preamble: The change of the voiced aspirated (breathy-voiced) velar plosive /gʱ/ to the glottal fricative /h/ is a debuccalization in which the oral closure is lost and only the breathy/aspirated component survives. It is best known from Indo-European: in Italic, PIE *gʰ and *ǵʰ passed through a fricative stage (Proto-Italic *χ) to Latin h (hostis, hiems); in Sanskrit, h continues PIE *ǵʰ and palatalized *gʰ/*gʷʰ via Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰʰ (hima-, hánti), while plain *gʰ stays gh; and in Middle Indo-Aryan (Prakrit) intervocalic Sanskrit gh was regularly reduced to h (megha > meha, laghu > lahu), a change inherited by modern Indo-Aryan languages. Other branches treat *gʰ differently (Greek kʰ, Germanic g, Slavic g), so the shift is well attested but not a default outcome; commonality is set to 4.

examples.note: 'stranger, enemy'; via Proto-Italic *hostis (*χ); cognate with Proto-Germanic *gastiz (English guest)
'winter'; Latin merges palatovelar *ǵʰ with plain *gʰ as h
'cold, frost, snow'; palatovelar *ǵʰ > Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰʰ > Sanskrit h; cognate with Latin hiems

'strikes, slays'; labiovelar *gʷʰ palatalized before *e to Proto-Indo-Iranian *ǰʰánti, then Sanskrit h (where no front vowel followed, the stop remains gh, cf. 3pl. ghnánti 'they strike' < *gʷʰn-énti)
Middle Indo-Aryan reduction of intervocalic aspirates to h; also Assamese meh, Gujarati meh, Punjabi mī̃h (Turner CDIAL 10302)
gh > h intervocalically; the Hindi form shows later metathesis lahu- > halu-
